## 5. The cube-digit principle and the exponent $19/27$

We now abandon the Vieta identity in favour of a construction whose injectivity is built in rather than deduced.

### 5.1 Greedy recovery

**Theorem 5.1 (Cube-digit uniqueness).** Let $z,r,z',r'$ be nonnegative integers with
$$r < 3z^2+3z+1, \qquad r' < 3z'^2+3z'+1, \qquad z^3+r = z'^3+r'.$$
Then $z=z'$ and $r=r'$.

*Proof.* The quantity $3z^2+3z+1$ is exactly the cube gap $(z+1)^3-z^3$. Suppose $z<z'$. Then
$$z^3 + r < z^3 + 3z^2+3z+1 = (z+1)^3 \le z'^3 \le z'^3+r',$$
contradicting the equality. Symmetrically $z'<z$ is impossible. Hence $z=z'$, and cancelling $z^3$ gives $r=r'$. $\square$

Equivalently: under the stated remainder bound, $z=\lfloor (z^3+r)^{1/3}\rfloor$, i.e. $z$ is the integer cube root of the value. This is a positional-notation principle with cubes as place values, which is why we call $z$ the leading *cube digit*.

Iterating once gives the engine used everywhere below.

**Theorem 5.2 (Two-step greedy injectivity).** Let $x,y,z,x',y',z'$ be nonnegative integers satisfying the four *gap conditions*
$$x^3<3y^2+3y+1,\quad x'^3<3y'^2+3y'+1,\quad x^3+y^3<3z^2+3z+1,\quad x'^3+y'^3<3z'^2+3z'+1,$$
and suppose $x^3+y^3+z^3 = x'^3+y'^3+z'^3$. Then $x=x'$, $y=y'$, $z=z'$.

*Proof sketch.* Rewrite the hypothesis as $z^3 + (x^3+y^3) = z'^3 + (x'^3+y'^3)$; the third and fourth gap conditions let Theorem 5.1 apply, giving $z=z'$ and $x^3+y^3 = x'^3+y'^3$. Rewrite the latter as $y^3+x^3 = y'^3+x'^3$; the first and second gap conditions let Theorem 5.1 apply again, giving $y=y'$ and $x^3=x'^3$, whence $x=x'$ since cubing is injective on $\mathbb{N}$. $\square$

Theorem 5.2 is reusable: *any* box of triples on which the four gap conditions hold carries an injective cube-sum map. The remaining design problem is to find a box that is as large as possible relative to the size of its values.

### 5.2 Scale analysis

The condition $x^3 \lesssim 3y^2$ says $x \lesssim y^{2/3}$; the condition $y^3 \lesssim 3z^2$ says $y\lesssim z^{2/3}$. Thus if $z$ ranges over a window of length $\asymp Z$, then $y$ may range over $\asymp Z^{2/3}$ values and $x$ over $\asymp Z^{4/9}$ values, so the box has
$$\asymp Z^{1+2/3+4/9} = Z^{19/9}$$
points while the values are of size $\asymp Z^3$. The exponent is therefore
$$\frac{19/9}{3} = \frac{19}{27}.$$
Choosing $Z = t^9$ clears all denominators: $z\asymp t^9$, $y\asymp t^6$, $x \asymp t^4$, box size $t^{4+6+9}=t^{19}$, values $\asymp t^{27}$.

### 5.3 The three-scale box

**Definition 5.3.** For $t\ge 1$ let
$$B(t) := \{\,(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{N}^3 : 1\le x\le t^4,\ \ t^6\le y<2t^6,\ \ 2t^9\le z<3t^9\,\}.$$

**Lemma 5.4 (Cardinality and positivity).** $\#B(t) = t^4\cdot t^6\cdot t^9 = t^{19}$, and every $(x,y,z)\in B(t)$ has $x,y,z\ge 1$.

*Proof.* The three ranges have $t^4$, $2t^6-t^6=t^6$, and $3t^9-2t^9=t^9$ elements. Positivity is immediate from $t\ge 1$. $\square$

**Lemma 5.5 (Gap conditions on the box).** Let $t\ge 1$ and $(x,y,z)\in B(t)$. Then
1. $x^3 < 3y^2+3y+1$;
2. $x^3+y^3 < 3z^2+3z+1$;
3. $x^3+y^3+z^3 \le 36\,t^{27}$.

*Proof sketch.*
(1) $x^3\le (t^4)^3 = t^{12}$ and $y\ge t^6$ gives $3y^2\ge 3t^{12} > t^{12}$.
(2) $x^3\le t^{12}\le t^{18}$ and $y^3<(2t^6)^3 = 8t^{18}$, so $x^3+y^3 < 9t^{18}$; meanwhile $z\ge 2t^9$ gives $3z^2\ge 12 t^{18} > 9t^{18}$. (This is why the $z$-window is placed at $[2t^9,3t^9)$ rather than at $[t^9,2t^9)$: the factor $4$ in $3z^2\ge 3\cdot 4t^{18}$ is what pays for the $8t^{18}$ from $y^3$.)
(3) $x^3\le t^{12}\le t^{27}$, $y^3<8t^{18}\le 8t^{27}$, $z^3<(3t^9)^3=27t^{27}$; summing, $x^3+y^3+z^3 \le 36 t^{27}$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.6 (Injectivity of the cube-digit family).** For every $t\ge 1$ the map
$$B(t)\longrightarrow \mathbb{N},\qquad (x,y,z)\longmapsto x^3+y^3+z^3$$
is injective.

*Proof.* Combine Lemma 5.5(1),(2) with Theorem 5.2. $\square$

Operationally, the inverse map is the greedy algorithm: given a value $n$ produced by the box, set $z=\lfloor n^{1/3}\rfloor$, then $y=\lfloor (n-z^3)^{1/3}\rfloor$, then $x=(n-z^3-y^3)^{1/3}$.

### 5.4 The counting theorem

**Definition.** For $N\in\mathbb{N}$ let
$$\mathcal{P}(N) := \{\,k\in\mathbb{Z} : 0<k\le N,\ k = x^3+y^3+z^3 \text{ with } x,y,z\ge 1 \,\},$$
the set of positive integers up to $N$ that are sums of three positive cubes. Note $\mathcal{P}(N)$ contains no padded-zero representations: each of its members is a fortiori a sum of three nonzero cubes, and $N\mapsto\#\mathcal{P}(N)$ is nondecreasing.

**Theorem 5.7 (Cube-digit counting theorem).** For every $t\ge 1$,
$$t^{19} \;\le\; \#\mathcal{P}\bigl(36\,t^{27}\bigr).$$

*Proof sketch.* Apply the cube-sum map to $B(t)$. By Theorem 5.6 the image has exactly $\#B(t)=t^{19}$ elements (Lemma 5.4); by Lemma 5.4 all coordinates are positive, so each image point is a sum of three positive cubes; by Lemma 5.5(3) each is at most $36t^{27}$; and each is positive. Hence the image is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(36t^{27})$ of size $t^{19}$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.8 (Beating the square-root barrier explicitly).** For every $t\ge 4$, with $N = 36t^{27}$,
$$100\,\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{N}\bigr\rfloor \;\le\; t^{19}.$$

*Proof sketch.* Since $t\ge 1$, $36t^{27}\le 36t^{28}=(6t^{14})^2$, so $\lfloor\sqrt{36t^{27}}\rfloor \le 6t^{14}$. Thus $100\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor \le 600\,t^{14}$. For $t\ge 4$ we have $t^5\ge 4^5 = 1024 \ge 600$, so $600t^{14}\le t^5\cdot t^{14} = t^{19}$. $\square$

Thus the cube-digit count exceeds any fixed multiple of $\sqrt{N}$ for all sufficiently large $N$ along the sample scales — the constant $100$ is arbitrary, and replacing it by $c$ only changes the threshold to $t\ge \max(4, \lceil (6c)^{1/5}\rceil)$.

**Theorem 5.9 (Real-analytic form at sample scales).** For every $t\ge 1$, with $N=36t^{27}$,
$$\frac{N^{19/27}}{36} \;\le\; \#\mathcal{P}(N).$$

*Proof sketch.* $N^{19/27} = 36^{19/27}\,(t^{27})^{19/27} = 36^{19/27}\,t^{19}\le 36\,t^{19}$, since $36^{19/27}\le 36^1$. Divide by $36$ and apply Theorem 5.7. $\square$

**Theorem 5.10 (Bound for all $N$).** For every integer $N\ge 36$,
$$\left(\frac{N}{36\cdot 2^{27}}\right)^{19/27} \;\le\; \#\mathcal{P}(N).$$

*Proof sketch.* Let $t := \lfloor (N/36)^{1/27}\rfloor$; since $N\ge 36$ we have $t\ge 1$.
*Lower approximation:* $t\le (N/36)^{1/27}$ gives $t^{27}\le N/36$, i.e. $36t^{27}\le N$, so by monotonicity of $\mathcal{P}$ and Theorem 5.7, $t^{19}\le \#\mathcal{P}(36t^{27}) \le \#\mathcal{P}(N)$.
*Upper approximation:* $(N/36)^{1/27} < t+1 \le 2t$ gives $N/36 < 2^{27}t^{27}$, i.e. $N/(36\cdot 2^{27}) \le t^{27}$.
Raising the last inequality to the power $19/27$ (monotone on nonnegative reals) gives $\left(N/(36\cdot 2^{27})\right)^{19/27}\le t^{19}$, and the chain closes. $\square$

Theorem 5.10 is the clean statement: the number of integers up to $N$ that are sums of three positive cubes is at least $c\,N^{19/27}$ with the explicit constant $c=(36\cdot 2^{27})^{-19/27}$, and $19/27 = 0.7037\ldots > 1/2$.

## 6. Escaping the Vieta family

The cube-digit family is quantitatively stronger. It is also qualitatively different: it reaches integers the Vieta identity provably cannot.

The key is Theorem 4.1: Vieta values are multiples of $6$. Since $n^3\equiv n \pmod 6$ for every integer $n$ (because $n^3-n=(n-1)n(n+1)$ is divisible by $6$), a sum of three cubes with all roots $\equiv 1 \pmod 6$ is $\equiv 3\pmod 6$, hence not a multiple of $6$, hence not a Vieta value.

It remains to check that the greedy machinery survives the residue restriction, with rescaled windows.

**Definition 6.1.** For $t\ge 1$ let
$$B^\ast(t) := \{\,(u,v,w)\in\mathbb{N}^3 : 1\le u\le t^4,\ \ 4t^6\le v<8t^6,\ \ 34t^9\le w<68t^9\,\},$$
and for $(u,v,w)\in B^\ast(t)$ set
$$E(u,v,w) := (6u+1)^3+(6v+1)^3+(6w+1)^3.$$

**Lemma 6.2.** Let $t\ge 1$ and $(u,v,w)\in B^\ast(t)$. Writing $X=6u+1$, $Y=6v+1$, $Z=6w+1$:
1. $\#B^\ast(t) = t^4\cdot 4t^6\cdot 34t^9 = 136\,t^{19}$;
2. $X^3 < 3Y^2+3Y+1$;
3. $X^3+Y^3 < 3Z^2+3Z+1$;
4. $E(u,v,w) \le 10^8\, t^{27}$;
5. $E(u,v,w)\equiv 3 \pmod 6$.

*Proof sketch.* (1) is a product of window lengths.
(2) $X\le 6t^4+1\le 7t^4$, so $X^3\le 343t^{12}$; while $Y\ge 24t^6$, so $3Y^2\ge 3\cdot 576\,t^{12}=1728\,t^{12}$.
(3) $X^3\le 343 t^{12}\le 343 t^{18}$ and $Y< 48t^6$ gives $Y^3<110592\,t^{18}$, total $<110935\,t^{18}$; while $Z\ge 204t^9$ gives $3Z^2\ge 3\cdot 41616\,t^{18} = 124848\,t^{18}$.
(4) $X^3\le 343t^{27}$, $Y^3 < 110592\,t^{27}$, $Z^3 < (408t^9)^3 = 67\,917\,312\,t^{27}$; the total is below $10^8t^{27}$.
(5) Expanding, $(6n+1)^3 = 6(36n^3+18n^2+3n)+1$, so each cube is $\equiv 1 \pmod 6$ and the sum is $\equiv 3$. $\square$

**Theorem 6.3 (Escape theorem).** For every $t\ge 1$, the number of integers $k$ with $1\le k\le 10^8t^{27}$ such that
- $k$ is a sum of three *positive* cubes, and
- $k \ne V(a,b)$ for every pair of integers $(a,b)$,

is at least $136\,t^{19}$.

*Proof sketch.* By Lemma 6.2(2),(3) and the two-step greedy injectivity engine (Theorem 5.2), the map $(u,v,w)\mapsto E(u,v,w)$ is injective on $B^\ast(t)$ — the engine returns $6u+1=6u'+1$, etc., whence $u=u'$, $v=v'$, $w=w'$. By Lemma 6.2(1) the image has $136t^{19}$ elements. Each is positive, is a sum of the three positive cubes $(6u+1)^3,(6v+1)^3,(6w+1)^3$, and by Lemma 6.2(4) is at most $10^8t^{27}$. Finally by Lemma 6.2(5) each is $\equiv 3\pmod 6$, so $6\nmid k$, so by Corollary 4.2 no pair $(a,b)$ has $V(a,b)=k$. $\square$

With $N = 10^8 t^{27}$ this is again a bound of order $N^{19/27}$, now for integers *outside* the Vieta value set. In particular, no amount of refinement of the Vieta identity could ever have produced these numbers: the improvement of §5 is not an improvement of §2–§3 but a replacement of it.

---

## 7. The greedy cube tower: $s$ cubes and exponent $1-(2/3)^s$

The cube-digit principle is indifferent to the number of summands. We record the general theorem.

**Definition 7.1.** Say $n\in\mathbb{N}$ is a **sum of $s$ positive cubes** if there are integers $z_1,\dots,z_s\ge 1$ with $n = z_1^3+\cdots+z_s^3$. (For $s=0$ this means $n=0$.) For $s\ge 1$ and $N\in\mathbb{N}$ let
$$\mathcal{Q}_s(N) := \{\, n : 0<n\le N,\ n \text{ is a sum of } s \text{ positive cubes}\,\}.$$

**Definition 7.2 (Tower constants).** Set $C_0 := 1$ and $C_{s+1} := 8C_s^3 + C_s$. Thus $C_1 = 9$, $C_2 = 8\cdot 729+9 = 5841$, and so on; each $C_s\ge 1$.

**Theorem 7.3 (Greedy cube tower).** For every $s\ge 0$ and every $t\ge 1$ there is a finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ with
$$\#S \;\ge\; t^{\,3^s-2^s}, \qquad \text{every } n\in S \text{ a sum of } s \text{ positive cubes with } n < C_s\, t^{\,3^s}.$$

*Proof sketch (induction on $s$).* For $s=0$ take $S=\{0\}$: $\#S = 1 = t^{0}$ and $0 < C_0 t^{1}=t$.

For the inductive step, apply the hypothesis at *scale $t^2$*, obtaining $S'$ with $\#S'\ge (t^2)^{3^s-2^s}$ and every $m\in S'$ satisfying $m< C_s\,(t^2)^{3^s} = C_s t^{2\cdot 3^s}=:B$. Put $Z := C_s t^{3^s}$ and consider
$$S := \{\, z^3+m : Z\le z<2Z,\ m\in S'\,\}.$$
*Gap check:* for $z\ge Z$ we have $3z^2 \ge 3Z^2 = 3C_s^2 t^{2\cdot 3^s} \ge 3 C_s t^{2\cdot 3^s} = 3B > B > m$, so each $m$ is below the cube gap at its $z$. By Theorem 5.1 the pairs $(z,m)$ are recoverable from $z^3+m$, so
$$\#S = Z\cdot \#S' \;\ge\; C_s t^{3^s}\cdot t^{2(3^s-2^s)} \;\ge\; t^{\,3^{s+1}-2^{s+1}},$$
using $3^{s+1}-2^{s+1} = 3^s + 2(3^s-2^s)$ and $C_s\ge 1$.
*Size check:* $z^3+m < (2Z)^3 + B = 8C_s^3 t^{3^{s+1}} + C_s t^{2\cdot 3^s} \le (8C_s^3+C_s)\,t^{3^{s+1}} = C_{s+1}t^{3^{s+1}}$, using $2\cdot 3^s\le 3^{s+1}$.
*Representation check:* each element of $S$ is $z^3$ plus a sum of $s$ positive cubes, with $z\ge Z\ge 1$, hence a sum of $s+1$ positive cubes. $\square$

**Theorem 7.4 (Tower counting).** For every $s\ge 1$ and $t\ge 1$,
$$t^{\,3^s-2^s} \;\le\; \#\mathcal{Q}_s\bigl(C_s\,t^{\,3^s}\bigr).$$

In particular $t^5 \le \#\mathcal{Q}_2(C_2 t^9)$, $t^{19}\le \#\mathcal{Q}_3(C_3t^{27})$, and $t^{65}\le\#\mathcal{Q}_4(C_4t^{81})$.

**Definition 7.5.** The **tower exponent** is $\varepsilon_s := \dfrac{3^s-2^s}{3^s} = 1 - \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{s}$.

**Theorem 7.6 (Tower bound for all $N$; limiting exponent).** For every $s\ge 1$ and every $N\ge C_s$,
$$\left(\frac{N}{C_s\,2^{3^s}}\right)^{\varepsilon_s} \;\le\; \#\mathcal{Q}_s(N).$$
Moreover $\varepsilon_s \to 1$ as $s\to\infty$.

*Proof sketch.* The interpolation is as in Theorem 5.10: put $t=\lfloor (N/C_s)^{1/3^s}\rfloor \ge 1$; then $C_st^{3^s}\le N$ gives $t^{3^s-2^s}\le \#\mathcal{Q}_s(N)$ by monotonicity, while $(N/C_s)^{1/3^s}<t+1\le 2t$ gives $N/(C_s2^{3^s})\le t^{3^s}$, and raising to the power $\varepsilon_s\in(0,1]$ converts the latter into $\left(N/(C_s2^{3^s})\right)^{\varepsilon_s}\le t^{3^s-2^s}$. The limit is immediate from $(2/3)^s\to 0$. $\square$

The first exponents are
$$\varepsilon_1 = \tfrac13 \approx 0.333,\quad \varepsilon_2 = \tfrac59 \approx 0.556,\quad \varepsilon_3 = \tfrac{19}{27}\approx 0.704,\quad \varepsilon_4 = \tfrac{65}{81}\approx 0.802,\quad \varepsilon_5 = \tfrac{211}{243}\approx 0.868 .$$
Each new cube recovers two thirds of the remaining deficit $1-\varepsilon_s$. Note that $\varepsilon_1=1/3$ is sharp for one cube (there are exactly $\lfloor N^{1/3}\rfloor$ cubes up to $N$), which is a useful sanity check on the normalisation; for $s\ge 2$ the bound is certainly not sharp, since already $\mathcal{Q}_2$ is expected to have order $N/(\log N)^{c}$-type behaviour.

---

## 8. Discussion: why the Vieta exponent is stuck at $1/2$

It is worth isolating the structural reason the two halves of this paper reach different exponents, since it is a phenomenon common to many parametric-family counting arguments.

**The Vieta family fails for an arithmetic reason.** The parameter set $\{(a,b) : 0<3ab(a+b)\le N\}$ has $\asymp N^{2/3}$ points. Theorem 2.7 says the fibres of the value map have size at most $d(v)$, and on average $d(v)$ is $O(\log v)$, so morally the image should have size $\gg N^{2/3}/\log N$. But converting "on average small fibres" into a *proved* lower bound requires exhibiting a subfamily on which one can *certify* injectivity, and certification requires that the value determine the parameters. Since $a \mid v$, the natural certification strategies restrict $a$ to a set $\mathcal{A}$ on which $a$ is determined by $v$: powers of a fixed prime (as in §3.3), or smooth numbers, or values with a distinguished valuation. For any such $\mathcal{A}$ the count is
$$\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A},\,a\le N^{1/3}} \#\{b : 3ab(a+b)\le N\} \;\asymp\; \sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}} \sqrt{N/a},$$
and thinness of $\mathcal{A}$ makes $\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}} a^{-1/2}$ convergent. So the total is $\Theta(\sqrt N)$, and one has traded away exactly as much as one gained. This is a genuine "needs a different definition" failure: no rearrangement of the same idea escapes it.

**The cube-digit family succeeds for a metric reason.** Its injectivity does not depend on the arithmetic of the values at all — only on the *sizes* of the summands relative to the local gap between consecutive cubes. Gap conditions are inequalities, and inequalities can be arranged by construction. The price is that the family is no longer a polynomial identity: it is a lattice box, and its exponent $19/27$ is dictated by the geometry $x\lesssim y^{2/3}\lesssim z^{4/9}$ rather than by any identity.

**The two are complementary, and the second strictly dominates.** §6 makes this precise: the cube-digit family reaches a residue class ($3\bmod 6$) that the Vieta family provably cannot enter, while producing $\gg N^{19/27}$ values there.

**Where the truth lies.** For sums of three positive cubes the conjectural answer is $\gg N$ (a positive proportion of integers, subject to the mod-$9$ obstruction in the signed problem). The exponent $19/27$ is what greediness alone can certify. The gap $19/27 \to 1$ is exactly the gap between "constructed with recoverable digits" and "counted by an asymptotic method"; closing it requires genuinely analytic input (Diophantine/circle-method estimates for the number of representations), and no elementary injective family can close it, because an injective family that produced $\gg N$ values would in particular have to be non-sparse in every residue class.

---

## 9. Open problems and future work

**Problem 1 (Divisor-controlled Vieta density).** Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $c(\varepsilon)>0$ with
$$\#\{\,v : |v|\le N,\ v = 3ab(a+b) \text{ for some } a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\,\} \;\ge\; c(\varepsilon)\,N^{2/3-\varepsilon}.$$
The route is Theorem 2.7: the $\asymp N^{2/3}$ lattice points collapse only by the divisor function, so any sub-polynomial divisor bound $d(v)\ll_\varepsilon v^{\varepsilon}$ turns the lattice count directly into the stated bound. The required divisor estimate is elementary multiplicative-function theory; nothing deeper (Thue equations, class field theory) is needed for the $2/3-\varepsilon$ exponent.

**Problem 2 (Exact Vieta asymptotics).** Determine $\kappa$ with
$$\#\{\,v : |v|\le N,\ v \text{ a Vieta value}\,\} \sim \kappa\,N^{2/3}.$$
Numerically the positive side has density constant $\approx 0.53$, suggesting $\kappa\approx 1.05$ after doubling for signs. A proof would presumably combine the divisor bound with an inclusion–exclusion over the multiplicity strata $\{v : \text{exactly } j \text{ representations}\}$.

**Problem 3 (Optimal greedy exponent for three cubes).** Is $19/27$ optimal for *greedy-recoverable* families? The gap conditions force $x \ll y^{2/3}$ and $y\ll z^{2/3}$, so $19/27$ is optimal within the class of "one window per summand". Relaxing to partially overlapping windows — where the greedy peel is replaced by a bounded search among $O(1)$ candidate leading digits — should allow $y$ up to $z^{2/3+\delta}$ at the cost of a bounded multiplicity, and might push the exponent slightly beyond $19/27$ while keeping the count injective up to a constant factor.

**Problem 4 (Escape in every admissible residue class).** §6 escapes the Vieta family through the class $3\bmod 6$. Which residue classes mod $9$ (the natural modulus for cubes) admit cube-digit families, and with which exponents? Since $n^3\in\{0,\pm 1\}\pmod 9$, a sum of three cubes is never $\equiv \pm 4\pmod 9$; the construction of §6 should adapt to give $\gg N^{19/27}$ representatives in each of the seven admissible classes.

**Problem 5 (Tower with mixed exponents).** The tower of §7 uses cubes at every level. The same greedy principle works for sums $z_1^{k_1}+\cdots+z_s^{k_s}$ with mixed exponents, the gap at level $j$ being $\asymp z_j^{k_j-1}$. Optimising the resulting exponent over $(k_1,\dots,k_s)$ subject to a size constraint is a clean finite-dimensional optimisation whose answer is not obvious.

**Problem 6 (Effective inverse).** The greedy peel is an $O(1)$-arithmetic-operation inverse to the cube-digit map (three integer cube roots). Can it be extended to a *decision* procedure for a positive-density set of integers — that is, a family of easily-recognised integers, defined by inequalities on their cube digits, all of which are certified sums of three positive cubes?

---

## 10. Conclusion

Two lessons emerge. First, the classical Vieta identity, although it produces sums of three cubes effortlessly and in a two-parameter family, is intrinsically limited as a counting device: its collisions are divisor collisions, so certifying injectivity costs exactly the factor one is trying to gain, and its values are confined to multiples of $6$. The best certified bound from it is $\lfloor\sqrt{N/6}\rfloor$, against an empirical truth of order $0.53\,N^{2/3}$ and a trivial ceiling of $\lfloor N/6\rfloor$.

Second, injectivity is cheaper to *build* than to *prove*. The cube-digit principle — a number of the form $z^3+r$ with $r$ below the cube gap $3z^2+3z+1$ determines $z$ and $r$ — turns positional notation into a construction principle for sums of cubes. Three nested windows at scales $t^4$, $t^6$, $t^9$ give $t^{19}$ distinct sums of three positive cubes below $36t^{27}$, hence at least $\left(N/(36\cdot 2^{27})\right)^{19/27}$ such integers below any $N\ge 36$; $s$ nested windows give the exponent $1-(2/3)^s$, increasing to $1$. And a residue-restricted version of the same box produces $\gg N^{19/27}$ integers which are sums of three positive cubes but which the Vieta identity can never reach at all.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}

Let $\mathcal{C}_3=\{n\in\Z : n=x^3+y^3+z^3,\ x,y,z\in\Z\}$. Deciding membership
in $\mathcal{C}_3$ for a specific $n$ is notoriously delicate; the only known
local obstruction is $n\not\equiv\pm 4\pmod 9$, and it is conjectured that every
other integer belongs to $\mathcal{C}_3$. Representations, when they exist, can
be enormous.

The counting problem is more tractable but still open in essentials. Write
$R_3(N)=\#\{n : 1\le n\le N,\ n\in\mathcal{C}_3\}$; conjecturally $R_3(N)\gg N$.
Unconditionally, the classical elementary route to lower bounds is to exhibit a
\emph{parametric family}: a polynomial identity in several parameters, all of
whose values lie in $\mathcal{C}_3$, together with an injectivity statement
turning the number of parameter choices into a lower bound for the number of
values.

Two rules of hygiene are respected throughout.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{No padded zeros.} A ``sum of three cubes'' with one cube equal to
$0^3$ is really a sum of two cubes. Every representation constructed below uses
three nonzero cubes; in the cube-digit families all three cubes are positive.
\item \textbf{Honest counting.} All counts are cardinalities of explicitly
defined sets of \emph{integers}, not of parameter tuples; injectivity is proved,
not assumed.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{The Vieta identity}

If $a+b+c=0$ then $a^3+b^3+c^3=3abc$; taking $c=-a-b$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:vieta}
a^3+b^3+(-a-b)^3=-3ab(a+b)=:V(a,b).
\end{equation}
The region $|3ab(a+b)|\le N$ contains $\asymp N^{2/3}$ lattice points, so a naive
count suggests $\asymp N^{2/3}$ distinct values; numerically, the number of
\emph{positive} integers $\le N$ of the form $3ab(a+b)$ is $\approx 0.53\,N^{2/3}$.
Proving anything of the sort is another matter, and Sections \ref{sec:collisions}
and \ref{sec:subfamilies} explain exactly why.

\section{The Vieta value map and its collisions}\label{sec:collisions}

\begin{definition}
For $a,b\in\Z$ set $V(a,b):=-3ab(a+b)$. Call $k\in\Z$ \emph{Vieta represented} if
there are $a,b\in\Z$ with $a\ne 0$, $b\ne0$, $a+b\ne 0$ and $V(a,b)=k$. Call $k$ a
\emph{sum of three nonzero cubes} if $k=x^3+y^3+z^3$ with $x,y,z$ nonzero integers.
\end{definition}

The nondegeneracy conditions are exactly what is needed for the three roots
$a,b,-a-b$ in \eqref{eq:vieta} to be nonzero; hence every Vieta represented
integer is a sum of three nonzero cubes. Also $V(-a,-b)=-V(a,b)$, so the family
is closed under sign change.

\begin{theorem}[Six-fold symmetry]\label{thm:symmetry}
For all $a,b\in\Z$,
\[
V(a,b)=V(b,a)=V(a,-a-b)=V(-a-b,a)=V(b,-a-b)=V(-a-b,b).
\]
If $a$, $b$, $-a-b$ are pairwise distinct these six parameter pairs are pairwise
distinct, so $V$ is at least six-to-one at such points.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each identity is verified by expansion. Conceptually $V(a,b)=3abc$ up to sign with
$c=-a-b$, and the substitutions realise the $S_3$-action permuting
$\{a,b,c\}$; the stabiliser of an ordered pair is trivial when the three roots are
distinct. Distinctness of the six pairs is a finite check.
\end{proof}

One quotients out this symmetry by restricting to the fundamental domain
$1\le a\le b$. That is not enough.

\begin{theorem}[No ordering restriction suffices]\label{thm:collision}
$V$ is not injective on $\{(a,b):1\le a\le b\}$:
\[
V(1,5)=V(2,3)=-90,\qquad (1,5)\ne(2,3),
\]
concretely $1^3+5^3+(-6)^3=-90=2^3+3^3+(-5)^3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$-3\cdot1\cdot5\cdot6=-90=-3\cdot2\cdot3\cdot5$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Scaling the spine by cubes, $(m,b)\mapsto 3m^3b(b+1)$, does not help either:
$3\cdot1^3\cdot15\cdot16=720=3\cdot2^3\cdot5\cdot6$.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Monotonicity in the second variable]\label{lem:mono}
For each fixed integer $a\ge1$ the map $b\mapsto 3ab(a+b)$ is strictly increasing
on $b\ge 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$b\mapsto b(a+b)$ is strictly increasing for $b\ge0$, $a\ge1$, and multiplication
by $3a>0$ preserves strict order.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Divisor bound for multiplicity]\label{thm:divisor}
For $v\ge1$,
\[
\#\{(a,b)\in\Z_{\ge1}^2 : 3ab(a+b)=v\}\ \le\ d(v),
\]
where $d(v)$ is the number of positive divisors of $v$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $3ab(a+b)=v$ with $a,b\ge1$ then $v=a\cdot\bigl(3b(a+b)\bigr)$, so $a\mid v$:
the first-coordinate projection maps solutions into $\mathrm{Div}(v)$. It is
injective by Lemma \ref{lem:mono}: two solutions with the same $a$ satisfy
$3ab(a+b)=3ab'(a+b')$, forcing $b=b'$.
\end{proof}

Theorem \ref{thm:divisor} makes precise the slogan \emph{collisions are divisor
collisions}. It is simultaneously encouraging (the $N^{2/3}$ lattice points
collapse only by a factor that is $v^{o(1)}$ on average) and cautionary (to
certify injectivity one must control which $a$ occur, and sparsifying $a$ costs a
full power).

\section{Injective subfamilies and square-root counting}\label{sec:subfamilies}

\begin{definition}
For $N\in\N$ put
\[
\mathcal{R}(N):=\{k\in\Z: 0<k\le N,\ k\text{ Vieta represented}\},\quad
\mathcal{R}^{\pm}(N):=\{k\in\Z: k\ne0,\ |k|\le N,\ k\text{ Vieta represented}\}.
\]
Both are finite and consist of sums of three nonzero cubes.
\end{definition}

\subsection{The spine}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{spine} is $S(b):=3b(b+1)$ for $b\ge1$; it equals $-V(-1,-b)$ and is
realised by $(-1)^3+(-b)^3+(1+b)^3=3b(b+1)$. It is strictly increasing, hence
injective.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Square-root lower bound]\label{thm:spine}
If $3m(m+1)\le N$ then $m\le\#\mathcal{R}(N)$. Consequently for every $N$,
\[
\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{N/6}\bigr\rfloor\ \le\ \#\mathcal{R}(N).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$S(1)<\dots<S(m)$ are $m$ distinct positive integers, each Vieta represented with
three nonzero cubes and each $\le S(m)=3m(m+1)\le N$. For the second statement
take $m=\lfloor\sqrt{N/6}\rfloor$, so $6m^2\le N$; since $3m(m+1)\le 6m^2$ for
$m\ge1$, the hypothesis holds ($m=0$ being trivial).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-sided bound]\label{thm:twosided}
If $3m(m+1)\le N$ then $2m\le\#\mathcal{R}^{\pm}(N)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both $S(b)$ and $-S(b)$ are Vieta represented, by $V(-a,-b)=-V(a,b)$; the two
families are disjoint since $S(b)>0$, and each is injective in $b$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The dyadic family}

\begin{definition}
For $i\ge1$ and odd $b\ge1$ put $D(i,b):=3\cdot2^i\,b\,(2^i+b)=-V(-2^i,-b)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[The valuation reads the layer]\label{lem:val}
If $i\ge1$ and $b\ge1$ is odd then $v_2\bigl(D(i,b)\bigr)=i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$D(i,b)=2^i\cdot\bigl(3b(2^i+b)\bigr)$; as $2^i$ is even and $b$ odd, $2^i+b$ is
odd, so $3b(2^i+b)$ is odd.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity of the dyadic family]\label{thm:dyadic}
If $i,j\ge1$ and $b,c\ge1$ are odd with $D(i,b)=D(j,c)$, then $i=j$ and $b=c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Lemma \ref{lem:val} gives $i=j$; then Lemma \ref{lem:mono} with $a=2^i$ gives $b=c$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-parameter count]\label{thm:dyadiccount}
For all $I,m\in\N$,
\[
I\cdot m\ \le\ \#\mathcal{R}\bigl(6\cdot2^I m(2^I+2m)\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Use the $Im$ pairs $(i,2p+1)$ with $1\le i\le I$, $0\le p<m$. The values are
distinct by Theorem \ref{thm:dyadic}, positive, Vieta represented with three
nonzero cubes, and bounded by $3\cdot2^I\cdot2m\cdot(2^I+2m)$.
\end{proof}

Optimising in $I$ and $m$ still yields only order $\sqrt{N}$: the family has
$I\asymp\log$ layers, each contributing $\asymp\sqrt{N}/2^{I}$ points.

\section{The Vieta ceiling}

\begin{theorem}[Divisibility by six]\label{thm:six}
$6\mid V(a,b)$ for all $a,b\in\Z$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$-3ab(a+b)$ is divisible by $3$. If $a$ or $b$ is even then $2\mid ab(a+b)$; if
both are odd then $a+b$ is even. Hence $2\mid ab(a+b)$ and $6\mid V(a,b)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:notvieta}
An integer not divisible by $6$ is not a Vieta value.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Ceiling and sandwich]\label{thm:sandwich}
For all $N$,
\[
\bigl\lfloor\sqrt{N/6}\bigr\rfloor\ \le\ \#\mathcal{R}(N)\ \le\ \Bigl\lfloor\frac{N}{6}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem \ref{thm:six} the set $\mathcal{R}(N)$ consists of positive multiples of
$6$ not exceeding $N$; there are $\lfloor N/6\rfloor$ of these. The lower bound is
Theorem \ref{thm:spine}.
\end{proof}

\section{The cube-digit principle and the exponent \texorpdfstring{$19/27$}{19/27}}

\subsection{Greedy recovery}

\begin{theorem}[Cube-digit uniqueness]\label{thm:cubedigit}
Let $z,r,z',r'\in\N$ with $r<3z^2+3z+1$, $r'<3z'^2+3z'+1$ and $z^3+r=z'^3+r'$.
Then $z=z'$ and $r=r'$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$3z^2+3z+1=(z+1)^3-z^3$ is the cube gap. If $z<z'$ then
$z^3+r<(z+1)^3\le z'^3\le z'^3+r'$, a contradiction; symmetrically $z'<z$ is
impossible. Hence $z=z'$, and cancelling gives $r=r'$.
\end{proof}

Equivalently, $z=\lfloor(z^3+r)^{1/3}\rfloor$: the value announces its leading
\emph{cube digit}.

\begin{theorem}[Two-step greedy injectivity]\label{thm:engine}
Let $x,y,z,x',y',z'\in\N$ satisfy the four gap conditions
\[
x^3<3y^2+3y+1,\quad x'^3<3y'^2+3y'+1,\quad
x^3+y^3<3z^2+3z+1,\quad x'^3+y'^3<3z'^2+3z'+1,
\]
and $x^3+y^3+z^3=x'^3+y'^3+z'^3$. Then $x=x'$, $y=y'$, $z=z'$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write the hypothesis as $z^3+(x^3+y^3)=z'^3+(x'^3+y'^3)$ and apply Theorem
\ref{thm:cubedigit} to get $z=z'$ and $x^3+y^3=x'^3+y'^3$; rewrite the latter as
$y^3+x^3=y'^3+x'^3$ and apply Theorem \ref{thm:cubedigit} again to get $y=y'$ and
$x^3=x'^3$, hence $x=x'$.
\end{proof}

Theorem \ref{thm:engine} is reusable: any box of triples satisfying the gap
conditions carries an injective cube-sum map.

\subsection{Scale analysis and the three-scale box}

The condition $x^3\lesssim 3y^2$ means $x\lesssim y^{2/3}$, and $y^3\lesssim 3z^2$
means $y\lesssim z^{2/3}$. If $z$ ranges over a window of length $\asymp Z$, the
box has $\asymp Z^{1+2/3+4/9}=Z^{19/9}$ points while values are $\asymp Z^3$,
giving the exponent $\tfrac{19/9}{3}=\tfrac{19}{27}$. Taking $Z=t^9$ clears
denominators.

\begin{definition}
For $t\ge1$ let
$B(t):=\{(x,y,z)\in\N^3 : 1\le x\le t^4,\ t^6\le y<2t^6,\ 2t^9\le z<3t^9\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:boxcard}
$\#B(t)=t^4\cdot t^6\cdot t^9=t^{19}$, and every point of $B(t)$ has all
coordinates $\ge 1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Gap conditions on the box]\label{lem:boxgaps}
Let $t\ge1$ and $(x,y,z)\in B(t)$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x^3<3y^2+3y+1$;
\item $x^3+y^3<3z^2+3z+1$;
\item $x^3+y^3+z^3\le 36\,t^{27}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(1) $x^3\le t^{12}$ while $3y^2\ge 3t^{12}$.
(2) $x^3+y^3\le t^{12}+8t^{18}<9t^{18}$ while $3z^2\ge 12t^{18}$. (This is why the
$z$-window starts at $2t^9$: the factor $4$ in $3z^2$ pays for the $8t^{18}$ from
$y^3$.)
(3) $x^3\le t^{27}$, $y^3<8t^{27}$, $z^3<27t^{27}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity of the cube-digit family]\label{thm:injbox}
For every $t\ge1$ the map $B(t)\to\N$, $(x,y,z)\mapsto x^3+y^3+z^3$, is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Lemma \ref{lem:boxgaps}(1),(2) with Theorem \ref{thm:engine}.
\end{proof}

The inverse is the greedy peel: $z=\lfloor n^{1/3}\rfloor$, then
$y=\lfloor(n-z^3)^{1/3}\rfloor$, then $x=(n-z^3-y^3)^{1/3}$.

\subsection{The counting theorem}

\begin{definition}
For $N\in\N$ let $\mathcal{P}(N):=\{k\in\Z : 0<k\le N,\ k=x^3+y^3+z^3
\text{ with } x,y,z\ge1\}$, the set of positive integers up to $N$ that are sums
of three positive cubes. Every member is a fortiori a sum of three nonzero cubes,
and $N\mapsto\#\mathcal{P}(N)$ is nondecreasing.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Cube-digit counting theorem]\label{thm:count}
For every $t\ge1$, \ $t^{19}\le\#\mathcal{P}(36\,t^{27})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply the cube-sum map to $B(t)$: by Theorem \ref{thm:injbox} and Lemma
\ref{lem:boxcard} the image has $t^{19}$ elements, all positive, all sums of three
positive cubes, all $\le36t^{27}$ by Lemma \ref{lem:boxgaps}(3).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Beating the square-root barrier]\label{thm:beats}
For $t\ge4$ and $N=36t^{27}$, \ $100\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\le t^{19}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$36t^{27}\le36t^{28}=(6t^{14})^2$, so $\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\le 6t^{14}$ and
$100\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\le 600t^{14}$; for $t\ge4$, $t^5\ge1024\ge600$, so
$600t^{14}\le t^{19}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Real form at sample scales]\label{thm:rpow}
For $t\ge1$ and $N=36t^{27}$, \ $N^{19/27}/36\le\#\mathcal{P}(N)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$N^{19/27}=36^{19/27}t^{19}\le 36\,t^{19}$; divide by $36$ and use Theorem
\ref{thm:count}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bound for all $N$]\label{thm:general}
For every integer $N\ge36$,
\[
\left(\frac{N}{36\cdot2^{27}}\right)^{19/27}\ \le\ \#\mathcal{P}(N).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Put $t:=\lfloor(N/36)^{1/27}\rfloor\ge1$. From $t\le(N/36)^{1/27}$ we get
$36t^{27}\le N$, so by monotonicity and Theorem \ref{thm:count},
$t^{19}\le\#\mathcal{P}(N)$. From $(N/36)^{1/27}<t+1\le2t$ we get
$N/(36\cdot2^{27})\le t^{27}$; raising to the power $19/27$ gives
$\bigl(N/(36\cdot2^{27})\bigr)^{19/27}\le t^{19}$.
\end{proof}

Thus $\#\mathcal{P}(N)\ge c\,N^{19/27}$ with the explicit constant
$c=(36\cdot2^{27})^{-19/27}$, and $19/27=0.7037\ldots>1/2$.

\section{Escaping the Vieta family}

Since $n^3-n=(n-1)n(n+1)$ is divisible by $6$, we have $n^3\equiv n\pmod 6$; hence
a sum of three cubes with all roots $\equiv1\pmod6$ is $\equiv3\pmod6$, so not a
multiple of $6$, so (Corollary \ref{cor:notvieta}) not a Vieta value. It remains to
check that the greedy machinery survives the residue restriction.

\begin{definition}
For $t\ge1$ let
\[
B^{\ast}(t):=\{(u,v,w)\in\N^3 : 1\le u\le t^4,\ 4t^6\le v<8t^6,\ 34t^9\le w<68t^9\},
\]
and for such $(u,v,w)$ put $E(u,v,w):=(6u+1)^3+(6v+1)^3+(6w+1)^3$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:escbox}
Let $t\ge1$, $(u,v,w)\in B^{\ast}(t)$, and write $X=6u+1$, $Y=6v+1$, $Z=6w+1$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\#B^{\ast}(t)=t^4\cdot4t^6\cdot34t^9=136\,t^{19}$;
\item $X^3<3Y^2+3Y+1$;
\item $X^3+Y^3<3Z^2+3Z+1$;
\item $E(u,v,w)\le 10^{8}t^{27}$;
\item $E(u,v,w)\equiv3\pmod6$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(2) $X\le7t^4$ so $X^3\le343t^{12}$, while $Y\ge24t^6$ so $3Y^2\ge1728t^{12}$.
(3) $X^3+Y^3\le 343t^{18}+110592t^{18}<110935t^{18}$, while $Z\ge204t^9$ gives
$3Z^2\ge124848\,t^{18}$.
(4) $X^3\le343t^{27}$, $Y^3<110592t^{27}$, $Z^3<(408t^9)^3=67\,917\,312\,t^{27}$.
(5) $(6n+1)^3=6(36n^3+18n^2+3n)+1\equiv1\pmod 6$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Escape theorem]\label{thm:escape}
For every $t\ge1$, the number of integers $k$ with $1\le k\le10^{8}t^{27}$ which
are sums of three \emph{positive} cubes and satisfy $k\ne V(a,b)$ for \emph{every}
pair of integers $(a,b)$ is at least $136\,t^{19}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma \ref{lem:escbox}(2),(3) and Theorem \ref{thm:engine} the map
$(u,v,w)\mapsto E(u,v,w)$ is injective on $B^{\ast}(t)$ (the engine returns
$6u+1=6u'+1$, hence $u=u'$, and likewise for $v,w$). Its image has $136t^{19}$
elements by (1), each positive, each a sum of three positive cubes, each
$\le10^8t^{27}$ by (4), and each $\equiv3\pmod6$ by (5); Corollary
\ref{cor:notvieta} finishes.
\end{proof}

With $N=10^8t^{27}$ this is again of order $N^{19/27}$, now for integers outside
the Vieta value set entirely: the construction of the previous section is not a
refinement of the Vieta family but a replacement of it.

\section{The greedy cube tower}

\begin{definition}
Call $n\in\N$ a \emph{sum of $s$ positive cubes} if $n=z_1^3+\dots+z_s^3$ with all
$z_j\ge1$ (for $s=0$: $n=0$). For $s\ge1$ let
$\mathcal{Q}_s(N):=\{n : 0<n\le N,\ n \text{ a sum of } s \text{ positive cubes}\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
Set $C_0:=1$ and $C_{s+1}:=8C_s^3+C_s$; thus $C_1=9$, $C_2=5841$, and $C_s\ge1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Greedy cube tower]\label{thm:tower}
For every $s\ge0$ and $t\ge1$ there is a finite $S\subseteq\N$ with
$\#S\ge t^{\,3^s-2^s}$ such that every $n\in S$ is a sum of $s$ positive cubes and
satisfies $n<C_s t^{\,3^s}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $s$. For $s=0$ take $S=\{0\}$.

For the step, apply the hypothesis at scale $t^2$, giving $S'$ with
$\#S'\ge(t^2)^{3^s-2^s}$ and $m<C_s t^{2\cdot3^s}=:B$ for all $m\in S'$. Put
$Z:=C_s t^{3^s}$ and $S:=\{z^3+m : Z\le z<2Z,\ m\in S'\}$.

\emph{Gap check.} For $z\ge Z$, $3z^2\ge3C_s^2t^{2\cdot3^s}\ge3B>B>m$, so Theorem
\ref{thm:cubedigit} makes $(z,m)$ recoverable from $z^3+m$; hence
\[
\#S=Z\cdot\#S'\ \ge\ C_s t^{3^s}\cdot t^{2(3^s-2^s)}\ \ge\ t^{\,3^{s+1}-2^{s+1}},
\]
using $3^{s+1}-2^{s+1}=3^s+2(3^s-2^s)$ and $C_s\ge1$.

\emph{Size check.} $z^3+m<(2Z)^3+B=8C_s^3t^{3^{s+1}}+C_st^{2\cdot3^s}
\le(8C_s^3+C_s)t^{3^{s+1}}=C_{s+1}t^{3^{s+1}}$.

\emph{Representation check.} Each element is $z^3$ with $z\ge1$ plus a sum of $s$
positive cubes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tower counting]\label{thm:towercount}
For $s\ge1$ and $t\ge1$, \ $t^{\,3^s-2^s}\le\#\mathcal{Q}_s\bigl(C_s t^{\,3^s}\bigr)$.
In particular $t^{5}\le\#\mathcal{Q}_2(C_2t^{9})$,
$t^{19}\le\#\mathcal{Q}_3(C_3t^{27})$, $t^{65}\le\#\mathcal{Q}_4(C_4t^{81})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{tower exponent} is
$\varepsilon_s:=\dfrac{3^s-2^s}{3^s}=1-\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{s}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Tower bound for all $N$; limiting exponent]\label{thm:towerrpow}
For $s\ge1$ and every $N\ge C_s$,
\[
\left(\frac{N}{C_s\,2^{3^s}}\right)^{\varepsilon_s}\ \le\ \#\mathcal{Q}_s(N),
\]
and $\varepsilon_s\to1$ as $s\to\infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Interpolate exactly as in Theorem \ref{thm:general}: with
$t=\lfloor(N/C_s)^{1/3^s}\rfloor\ge1$ one has $C_st^{3^s}\le N$ and
$N/(C_s2^{3^s})\le t^{3^s}$; raise the latter to the power
$\varepsilon_s\in(0,1]$. The limit follows from $(2/3)^s\to0$.
\end{proof}

The first exponents are
$\varepsilon_1=\tfrac13$, $\varepsilon_2=\tfrac59\approx0.556$,
$\varepsilon_3=\tfrac{19}{27}\approx0.704$,
$\varepsilon_4=\tfrac{65}{81}\approx0.802$,
$\varepsilon_5=\tfrac{211}{243}\approx0.868$: each new cube recovers two thirds of
the remaining deficit. The value $\varepsilon_1=1/3$ is sharp (there are
$\lfloor N^{1/3}\rfloor$ cubes up to $N$), a useful check on the normalisation.

\section{Discussion: why the Vieta exponent is stuck at \texorpdfstring{$1/2$}{1/2}}

\paragraph{Vieta fails for an arithmetic reason.}
The parameter region $\{(a,b):0<3ab(a+b)\le N\}$ has $\asymp N^{2/3}$ points, and
by Theorem \ref{thm:divisor} the fibres have size at most $d(v)$, which is
$O(\log v)$ on average; morally the image should have size $\gg N^{2/3}/\log N$.
Converting this into a proof requires a subfamily on which injectivity can be
\emph{certified}, and certification requires the value to determine the parameters.
Since $a\mid v$, the natural strategies restrict $a$ to a thin set $\mathcal{A}$
(powers of a fixed prime, smooth numbers, distinguished valuations). Then the count
is
\[
\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A},\,a\le N^{1/3}}\#\{b : 3ab(a+b)\le N\}\ \asymp\
\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\sqrt{N/a},
\]
and thinness makes $\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}a^{-1/2}$ converge: the total is
$\Theta(\sqrt N)$. One has traded away exactly what one gained.

\paragraph{The cube-digit family succeeds for a metric reason.}
Its injectivity does not depend on the arithmetic of the values, only on the sizes
of the summands relative to the local gap between consecutive cubes. Gap conditions
are inequalities, and inequalities can be arranged by construction. The price is
that the family is a lattice box rather than a polynomial identity, and its
exponent is dictated by the geometry $x\lesssim y^{2/3}\lesssim z^{4/9}$.

\paragraph{Where the truth lies.}
For sums of three positive cubes the conjectural answer is $\gg N$. The exponent
$19/27$ is what greediness alone can certify; closing the gap requires genuinely
analytic input, and no elementary injective family can close it, since a family
producing $\gg N$ values would have to be non-sparse in every residue class.

\section{Open problems}

\begin{problem}[Divisor-controlled Vieta density]
Show that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $c(\varepsilon)>0$ with
\[
\#\{v : |v|\le N,\ v=3ab(a+b)\ \text{for some } a,b\in\Z\}\ \ge\ c(\varepsilon)N^{2/3-\varepsilon}.
\]
By Theorem \ref{thm:divisor} the $\asymp N^{2/3}$ lattice points collapse only by
the divisor function, so any bound $d(v)\ll_\varepsilon v^{\varepsilon}$ suffices;
this is elementary multiplicative-function theory.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Exact Vieta asymptotics]
Determine $\kappa$ with $\#\{v : |v|\le N,\ v \text{ a Vieta value}\}\sim\kappa N^{2/3}$.
Numerically the positive side has constant $\approx0.53$, suggesting
$\kappa\approx1.05$.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Optimal greedy exponent]
Is $19/27$ optimal among greedy-recoverable families? Within the class of one
window per summand it is forced by $x\ll y^{2/3}$, $y\ll z^{2/3}$; allowing
partially overlapping windows, with a bounded search among $O(1)$ candidate leading
digits, might push the exponent slightly higher at the cost of bounded
multiplicity.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Escape in every admissible class]
A sum of three cubes is never $\equiv\pm4\pmod9$. Which of the seven admissible
classes mod $9$ admit cube-digit families, and with what exponents?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Mixed exponents]
The greedy principle applies to $z_1^{k_1}+\dots+z_s^{k_s}$, the gap at level $j$
being $\asymp z_j^{k_j-1}$. Optimise the resulting counting exponent over
$(k_1,\dots,k_s)$.
\end{problem}

\section{Conclusion}

The Vieta identity produces sums of three cubes effortlessly, but is intrinsically
limited as a counting device: its collisions are divisor collisions, so certifying
injectivity costs exactly the factor one is trying to gain, and its values are
confined to multiples of $6$. The best certified bound is $\lfloor\sqrt{N/6}\rfloor$,
against an empirical truth $\approx0.53\,N^{2/3}$ and a ceiling $\lfloor N/6\rfloor$.

Injectivity, however, is cheaper to build than to prove. The cube-digit principle
turns positional notation into a construction principle: three nested windows at
scales $t^4,t^6,t^9$ give $t^{19}$ distinct sums of three positive cubes below
$36t^{27}$, hence at least $\bigl(N/(36\cdot2^{27})\bigr)^{19/27}$ such integers
below any $N\ge36$; $s$ nested windows give the exponent $1-(2/3)^s\to1$; and a
residue-restricted box produces $\gg N^{19/27}$ integers which are sums of three
positive cubes but which the Vieta identity can never reach.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Set, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 0. Small integer utilities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def integer_cube_root(n: int) -> int:
    """Return floor(n ** (1/3)) for n >= 0, exactly, by Newton iteration."""
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("integer_cube_root expects a nonnegative integer")
    if n < 2:
        return n
    z = 1 << ((n.bit_length() + 2) // 3)
    while True:
        w = (2 * z + n // (z * z)) // 3
        if w >= z:
            break
        z = w
    while (z + 1) ** 3 <= n:
        z += 1
    while z**3 > n:
        z -= 1
    return z


def divisor_count(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of positive divisors of n >= 1 by trial division."""
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("divisor_count expects a positive integer")
    count, d = 0, 1
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            count += 2 if d * d != n else 1
        d += 1
    return count


def cube_gap(z: int) -> int:
    """(z+1)^3 - z^3 = 3z^2 + 3z + 1: the local gap between consecutive cubes."""
    return 3 * z * z + 3 * z + 1


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 1. The Vieta identity and its symmetries
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def vieta_value(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """V(a,b) = -3ab(a+b) = a^3 + b^3 + (-a-b)^3."""
    return -3 * a * b * (a + b)


def vieta_orbit(a: int, b: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """The S_3-orbit of (a,b) acting on the three roots {a, b, -a-b}."""
    c = -a - b
    return [(a, b), (b, a), (a, c), (c, a), (b, c), (c, b)]

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 2. Multiplicity is bounded by the divisor function
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def vieta_preimages(v: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """All (a,b) with a,b >= 1 and 3ab(a+b) = v (uses a | v and monotonicity)."""
    if v <= 0 or v % 3 != 0:
        return []
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    a = 1
    while 3 * a * 1 * (a + 1) <= v:
        if v % a == 0:
            # solve 3 a b (a+b) = v for b by bisection (strictly increasing in b)
            lo, hi = 1, 1
            while 3 * a * hi * (a + hi) < v:
                hi *= 2
            while lo <= hi:
                mid = (lo + hi) // 2
                val = 3 * a * mid * (a + mid)
                if val == v:
                    out.append((a, mid))
                    break
                if val < v:
                    lo = mid + 1
                else:
                    hi = mid - 1
        a += 1
    return out


def demo_divisor_bound(limit: int = 20000) -> None:
    print()

    for v in range(6, limit + 1, 6):
        pre = vieta_preimages(v)
        if len(pre) >= 2:
            worst.append((v, len(pre), divisor_count(v)))
    worst.sort(key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0]))
    print(f"  scanning v <= {limit}; values with multiplicity >= 2 (top 8):")
    print(f"    {'v':>8} {'#preimages':>11} {'d(v)':>6}   bound holds")
    for v, mult, dv in worst[:8]:

    ok = all(m <= d for _, m, d in worst)

    print(f"  values with >= 2 representations below {limit}: {len(worst)}")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 3. The Vieta ceiling and the empirical exponent 2/3
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def vieta_values_up_to(n_max: int) -> Set[int]:
    """All positive integers <= n_max of the form 3ab(a+b) with a,b >= 1."""
    out: Set[int] = set()
    a = 1
    while 3 * a * 1 * (a + 1) <= n_max:
        b = 1
        while True:
            v = 3 * a * b * (a + b)
            if v > n_max:
                break
            out.add(v)
            b += 1
        a += 1
    return out

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 4. The cube-digit principle
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def cube_digit_recover(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Given n = z^3 + r with r < 3z^2+3z+1, return (z, r): z = floor(n^(1/3))."""
    z = integer_cube_root(n)
    return z, n - z**3


def greedy_peel_three(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Invert the cube-digit map: recover (x,y,z) from n = x^3+y^3+z^3."""
    z, rest = cube_digit_recover(n)
    y, rest2 = cube_digit_recover(rest)
    x = integer_cube_root(rest2)
    return x, y, z

# Section 5. The three-scale box and the exponent 19/27

def box_points(t: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """The box  1 <= x <= t^4,  t^6 <= y < 2t^6,  2t^9 <= z < 3t^9."""
    for x in range(1, t**4 + 1):
        for y in range(t**6, 2 * t**6):
            for z in range(2 * t**9, 3 * t**9):
                yield (x, y, z)


def check_box(t: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Verify cardinality t^19, both gap conditions, value bound, injectivity."""
    pts = list(box_points(t))
    seen: Dict[int, Tuple[int, int, int]] = {}
    gaps_ok = True
    bound_ok = True
    peel_ok = True
    for (x, y, z) in pts:
        if not (x**3 < cube_gap(y)):
            gaps_ok = False
        if not (x**3 + y**3 < cube_gap(z)):
            gaps_ok = False
        n = x**3 + y**3 + z**3
        if n > 36 * t**27:
            bound_ok = False
        if greedy_peel_three(n) != (x, y, z):
            peel_ok = False
        seen.setdefault(n, (x, y, z))
    return {
        "t": t,
        "points": len(pts),
        "t^19": t**19,
        "distinct_values": len(seen),
        "injective": len(seen) == len(pts),
        "gap_conditions": gaps_ok,
        "value_bound_36t27": bound_ok,
        "greedy_peel_inverts": peel_ok,
        "max_value": max(seen) if seen else 0,
        "36t^27": 36 * t**27,
    }

def escape_points(t: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """The residue-restricted box  1<=u<=t^4, 4t^6<=v<8t^6, 34t^9<=w<68t^9."""
    for u in range(1, t**4 + 1):
        for v in range(4 * t**6, 8 * t**6):
            for w in range(34 * t**9, 68 * t**9):
                yield (u, v, w)


def escape_value(u: int, v: int, w: int) -> int:
    """(6u+1)^3 + (6v+1)^3 + (6w+1)^3: all three roots are 1 mod 6."""
    return (6 * u + 1) ** 3 + (6 * v + 1) ** 3 + (6 * w + 1) ** 3

def tower_const(s: int) -> int:
    """C_0 = 1,  C_{s+1} = 8 C_s^3 + C_s."""
    c = 1
    for _ in range(s):
        c = 8 * c**3 + c
    return c


def tower_exponent(s: int) -> float:
    """(3^s - 2^s)/3^s = 1 - (2/3)^s."""
    return (3**s - 2**s) / 3**s


def greedy_tower_set(s: int, t: int) -> Set[int]:
    """Constructive version of the tower: the set S of the induction."""
    if s == 0:
        return {0}
    prev = greedy_tower_set(s - 1, t * t)
    z0 = tower_const(s - 1) * t ** (3 ** (s - 1))
    return {z**3 + m for z in range(z0, 2 * z0) for m in prev}

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 0. Small integer utilities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def integer_cube_root(n: int) -> int:
    """Return floor(n ** (1/3)) for n >= 0, exactly, by Newton iteration."""
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("integer_cube_root expects a nonnegative integer")
    if n < 2:
        return n
    z = 1 << ((n.bit_length() + 2) // 3)
    while True:
        w = (2 * z + n // (z * z)) // 3
        if w >= z:
            break
        z = w
    while (z + 1) ** 3 <= n:
        z += 1
    while z**3 > n:
        z -= 1
    return z


def divisor_count(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of positive divisors of n >= 1 by trial division."""
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("divisor_count expects a positive integer")
    count, d = 0, 1
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            count += 2 if d * d != n else 1
        d += 1
    return count


def cube_gap(z: int) -> int:
    """(z+1)^3 - z^3 = 3z^2 + 3z + 1: the local gap between consecutive cubes."""
    return 3 * z * z + 3 * z + 1


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 1. The Vieta identity and its symmetries
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def vieta_value(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """V(a,b) = -3ab(a+b) = a^3 + b^3 + (-a-b)^3."""
    return -3 * a * b * (a + b)


def vieta_orbit(a: int, b: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """The S_3-orbit of (a,b) acting on the three roots {a, b, -a-b}."""
    c = -a - b
    return [(a, b), (b, a), (a, c), (c, a), (b, c), (c, b)]

def vieta_preimages(v: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """All (a,b) with a,b >= 1 and 3ab(a+b) = v (uses a | v and monotonicity)."""
    if v <= 0 or v % 3 != 0:
        return []
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    a = 1
    while 3 * a * 1 * (a + 1) <= v:
        if v % a == 0:
            # solve 3 a b (a+b) = v for b by bisection (strictly increasing in b)
            lo, hi = 1, 1
            while 3 * a * hi * (a + hi) < v:
                hi *= 2
            while lo <= hi:
                mid = (lo + hi) // 2
                val = 3 * a * mid * (a + mid)
                if val == v:
                    out.append((a, mid))
                    break
                if val < v:
                    lo = mid + 1
                else:
                    hi = mid - 1
        a += 1
    return out

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def vieta_values_up_to(n_max: int) -> Set[int]:
    """All positive integers <= n_max of the form 3ab(a+b) with a,b >= 1."""
    out: Set[int] = set()
    a = 1
    while 3 * a * 1 * (a + 1) <= n_max:
        b = 1
        while True:
            v = 3 * a * b * (a + b)
            if v > n_max:
                break
            out.add(v)
            b += 1

def cube_digit_recover(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Given n = z^3 + r with r < 3z^2+3z+1, return (z, r): z = floor(n^(1/3))."""
    z = integer_cube_root(n)
    return z, n - z**3


def greedy_peel_three(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Invert the cube-digit map: recover (x,y,z) from n = x^3+y^3+z^3."""
    z, rest = cube_digit_recover(n)
    y, rest2 = cube_digit_recover(rest)
    x = integer_cube_root(rest2)
    return x, y, z

def box_points(t: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """The box  1 <= x <= t^4,  t^6 <= y < 2t^6,  2t^9 <= z < 3t^9."""
    for x in range(1, t**4 + 1):
        for y in range(t**6, 2 * t**6):
            for z in range(2 * t**9, 3 * t**9):
                yield (x, y, z)


def check_box(t: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Verify cardinality t^19, both gap conditions, value bound, injectivity."""
    pts = list(box_points(t))
    seen: Dict[int, Tuple[int, int, int]] = {}
    gaps_ok = True
    bound_ok = True
    peel_ok = True
    for (x, y, z) in pts:
        if not (x**3 < cube_gap(y)):
            gaps_ok = False
        if not (x**3 + y**3 < cube_gap(z)):
            gaps_ok = False
        n = x**3 + y**3 + z**3
        if n > 36 * t**27:
            bound_ok = False
        if greedy_peel_three(n) != (x, y, z):
            peel_ok = False
        seen.setdefault(n, (x, y, z))
    return {
        "t": t,
        "points": len(pts),
        "t^19": t**19,
        "distinct_values": len(seen),
        "injective": len(seen) == len(pts),
        "gap_conditions": gaps_ok,
        "value_bound_36t27": bound_ok,
        "greedy_peel_inverts": peel_ok,
        "max_value": max(seen) if seen else 0,
        "36t^27": 36 * t**27,
    }

def tower_const(s: int) -> int:
    """C_0 = 1,  C_{s+1} = 8 C_s^3 + C_s."""
    c = 1
    for _ in range(s):
        c = 8 * c**3 + c
    return c


def tower_exponent(s: int) -> float:
    """(3^s - 2^s)/3^s = 1 - (2/3)^s."""
    return (3**s - 2**s) / 3**s


def greedy_tower_set(s: int, t: int) -> Set[int]:
    """Constructive version of the tower: the set S of the induction."""
    if s == 0:
        return {0}
    prev = greedy_tower_set(s - 1, t * t)
    z0 = tower_const(s - 1) * t ** (3 ** (s - 1))
    return {z**3 + m for z in range(z0, 2 * z0) for m in prev}

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Set, Tuple


def vieta_values_up_to(n_max: int) -> Set[int]:
    """All positive integers <= n_max of the form 3ab(a+b), a, b >= 1."""
    out: Set[int] = set()
    a = 1
    while 3 * a * (a + 1) <= n_max:
        b = 1
        while True:
            v = 3 * a * b * (a + b)
            if v > n_max:
                break
            out.add(v)
            b += 1
        a += 1
    return out


def counting_table(n_values: List[int]) -> List[Tuple[int, int, int, int, float]]:
    """For each N: (N, floor(sqrt(N/6)), #Vieta(N), floor(N/6), #/N^(2/3))."""
    rows = []
    for n in n_values:
        count = len(vieta_values_up_to(n))
        rows.append((n, math.isqrt(n // 6), count, n // 6,
                     count / n ** (2 / 3)))
    return rows


def fit_power_law(points: List[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Least-squares fit of log(count) = alpha log(N) + log(c); return (alpha, c)."""
    xs = [math.log(n) for n, _ in points]
    ys = [math.log(c) for _, c in points]
    m = len(xs)
    mean_x, mean_y = sum(xs) / m, sum(ys) / m
    num = sum((x - mean_x) * (y - mean_y) for x, y in zip(xs, ys))
    den = sum((x - mean_x) ** 2 for x in xs)
    alpha = num / den
    return alpha, math.exp(mean_y - alpha * mean_x)


def pair_count_up_to(n_max: int) -> int:
    """Number of parameter pairs (a, b), a, b >= 1, with 3ab(a+b) <= n_max.

    This is an upper bound for the size of the value set, and is itself of
    order N^(2/3); the ratio value-count / pair-count is the collapse factor
    caused by divisor-type collisions.
    """
    total = 0
    a = 1
    while 3 * a * (a + 1) <= n_max:
        b = 1
        while 3 * a * b * (a + b) <= n_max:
            total += 1
            b += 1
        a += 1
    return total

        print(f"{n:>10} {lo:>12} {count:>12} {hi:>12} {ratio:>11.4f} "

def escape_triples(t: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, int, int]]:

def certify_escape_sampled(t: int, samples: int = 20000, seed: int = 1) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Random-sample certification for a scale t too large to enumerate."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    seen: Dict[int, Tuple[int, int, int]] = {}
    gaps_ok = True
    bound_ok = True
    for _ in range(samples):
        u = rng.randrange(1, t**4 + 1)
        v = rng.randrange(4 * t**6, 8 * t**6)
        w = rng.randrange(34 * t**9, 68 * t**9)

        if not (big_x**3 < cube_gap(big_y)
                and big_x**3 + big_y**3 < cube_gap(big_z)):
            gaps_ok = False
        n = escape_value(u, v, w)
        if n > 10**8 * t**27:
            bound_ok = False
        if n in seen and seen[n] != (u, v, w):
            raise AssertionError("collision detected")
        seen[n] = (u, v, w)
    return {
        "t": t,
        "sampled triples": samples,
        "distinct values": len(seen),
        "gap conditions": gaps_ok,
        "within 10^8 t^27": bound_ok,
        "residues mod 6": sorted({n % 6 for n in seen}),
    }


def brute_force_vieta_hit(n: int) -> bool:
    """Search exhaustively for integers a, b with -3ab(a+b) = n (n > 0)."""
    limit = 1 + int(abs(n) ** (1 / 3)) * 4
    for a in range(-limit, limit + 1):
        for b in range(-limit, limit + 1):
            if -3 * a * b * (a + b) == n:
                return True
    return False

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Optional, Tuple


def integer_cube_root(n: int) -> int:
    """Exact floor(n^(1/3)) for n >= 0 via Newton's method on integers."""
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative input required")
    if n < 2:
        return n
    z = 1 << ((n.bit_length() + 2) // 3)
    while True:
        w = (2 * z + n // (z * z)) // 3
        if w >= z:
            break
        z = w
    while (z + 1) ** 3 <= n:
        z += 1
    while z**3 > n:
        z -= 1
    return z


def cube_gap(z: int) -> int:
    """The gap (z+1)^3 - z^3 = 3z^2 + 3z + 1 above the cube of z."""
    return 3 * z * z + 3 * z + 1


def cube_digit_step(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """One greedy step: n = z^3 + r with z = floor(n^(1/3)), r < cube_gap(z)."""
    z = integer_cube_root(n)
    return z, n - z**3


def greedy_decode_three(n: int, verify: bool = True) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """Recover (x, y, z) from n = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 when the gap conditions hold.

    Returns None if the greedy peel does not terminate in three exact cubes,
    i.e. if n was not produced by a cube-digit family.
    """
    z, rest = cube_digit_step(n)
    y, rest2 = cube_digit_step(rest)
    x = integer_cube_root(rest2)
    if x**3 != rest2:
        return None
    if verify:
        # the certificate: both nested gap conditions must hold
        if not (x**3 < cube_gap(y) and x**3 + y**3 < cube_gap(z)):
            return None
    return x, y, z

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Tuple


def cube_gap(z: int) -> int:
    """(z+1)^3 - z^3 = 3z^2 + 3z + 1."""
    return 3 * z * z + 3 * z + 1


def box_ranges(t: int) -> Tuple[range, range, range]:
    """The three nested windows: x in [1, t^4], y in [t^6, 2t^6), z in [2t^9, 3t^9)."""
    return (range(1, t**4 + 1), range(t**6, 2 * t**6), range(2 * t**9, 3 * t**9))


def gap_conditions_hold(t: int) -> bool:
    """Check the two nested gap conditions at the extreme corners of the box.

    Because x^3 is maximal at x = t^4, y^3 at y = 2t^6 - 1, and the gap terms are
    minimal at y = t^6 and z = 2t^9, testing the corners certifies the whole box.
    """
    x_max, y_min, y_max, z_min = t**4, t**6, 2 * t**6 - 1, 2 * t**9
    return (x_max**3 < cube_gap(y_min)
            and x_max**3 + y_max**3 < cube_gap(z_min))


def enumerate_box(t: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, int, int, int]]:
    """Yield (x, y, z, x^3+y^3+z^3) over the whole box."""
    rx, ry, rz = box_ranges(t)
    for x in rx:
        cx = x**3
        for y in ry:
            cxy = cx + y**3
            for z in rz:
                yield x, y, z, cxy + z**3


def certify_box(t: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Enumerate the box and certify cardinality, injectivity and the value bound."""
    seen: Dict[int, Tuple[int, int, int]] = {}
    count = 0
    max_value = 0
    for x, y, z, n in enumerate_box(t):
        count += 1
        max_value = max(max_value, n)
        if n in seen:
            raise AssertionError(f"collision: {seen[n]} and {(x, y, z)} both give {n}")
        seen[n] = (x, y, z)
    return {
        "t": t,
        "gap_conditions": gap_conditions_hold(t),
        "cardinality": count,
        "predicted_cardinality": t**19,
        "distinct_values": len(seen),
        "max_value": max_value,
        "value_bound": 36 * t**27,
        "bound_respected": max_value <= 36 * t**27,
    }


def certified_lower_bound(n_limit: int) -> float:
    """The certified count (N/(36*2^27))^(19/27) of sums of three positive cubes."""
    return (n_limit / (36 * 2**27)) ** (19 / 27)

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Tuple


def divisors(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All positive divisors of n >= 1, by trial division up to sqrt(n)."""
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("positive input required")
    small, large = [], []
    d = 1
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            small.append(d)
            if d * d != n:
                large.append(n // d)
        d += 1
    return small + large[::-1]


def solve_for_b(a: int, v: int) -> int:
    """The unique b >= 1 with 3ab(a+b) = v, or 0 if none exists.

    For fixed a >= 1 the map b -> 3ab(a+b) is strictly increasing, so binary
    search is exact and there is at most one solution.
    """
    lo, hi = 1, 1
    while 3 * a * hi * (a + hi) < v:
        hi *= 2
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        val = 3 * a * mid * (a + mid)
        if val == v:
            return mid
        if val < v:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return 0


def vieta_preimages(v: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """All ordered pairs (a, b) of positive integers with 3ab(a+b) = v.

    The search is restricted to divisors a of v -- which is legitimate because
    v = a * (3b(a+b)) -- so the loop runs at most d(v) times, which is exactly
    the divisor bound for the multiplicity of a Vieta value.
    """
    if v <= 0:
        return []
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for a in divisors(v):
        if 3 * a * (a + 1) > v:
            break
        b = solve_for_b(a, v)
        if b:
            out.append((a, b))
    return out


def multiplicity_report(v: int) -> str:
    pre = vieta_preimages(v)
    return (f"v = {v}: {len(pre)} representation(s) 3ab(a+b) = v, "
            f"d(v) = {len(divisors(v))}, divisor bound "
            f"{'holds' if len(pre) <= len(divisors(v)) else 'FAILS'}; {pre}")

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Set, Tuple


def tower_const(s: int) -> int:
    """C_0 = 1 and C_{s+1} = 8 C_s^3 + C_s: the size constant of level s."""
    c = 1
    for _ in range(s):
        c = 8 * c**3 + c
    return c


def tower_exponent(s: int) -> float:
    """(3^s - 2^s)/3^s = 1 - (2/3)^s."""
    return 1.0 - (2.0 / 3.0) ** s


def greedy_tower_set(s: int, t: int) -> Set[int]:
    """Build the level-s greedy family at scale t.

    Recursion: build the level-(s-1) family at scale t^2, then prepend a new
    leading cube z^3 with Z <= z < 2Z, Z = C_{s-1} t^(3^(s-1)).  Every previous
    value is below B = C_{s-1} t^(2*3^(s-1)) <= 3 Z^2 / 3, hence below the cube
    gap at z, so the greedy peel recovers z and the tail.
    """
    if s == 0:
        return {0}
    tail = greedy_tower_set(s - 1, t * t)
    z0 = tower_const(s - 1) * t ** (3 ** (s - 1))
    return {z**3 + m for z in range(z0, 2 * z0) for m in tail}


def tower_report(s: int, t: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int, int]:
    """Return (|S|, predicted t^(3^s-2^s), max value, bound C_s t^(3^s))."""
    S = greedy_tower_set(s, t)
    return len(S), t ** (3**s - 2**s), max(S), tower_const(s) * t ** (3**s)


def certified_lower_bound(s: int, n_limit: float) -> float:
    """(N / (C_s 2^(3^s)))^(1-(2/3)^s), valid for N >= C_s."""
    base = n_limit / (tower_const(s) * 2 ** (3**s))
    return base ** tower_exponent(s) if base > 0 else 0.0

def vieta_values_up_to(n_max: int) -> Set[int]:
    out: Set[int] = set()
    a = 1
    while 3 * a * (a + 1) <= n_max:
        b = 1
        while True:
            v = 3 * a * b * (a + b)
            if v > n_max:
                break
            out.add(v)
            b += 1
        a += 1
    return out

    c = 1
    for _ in range(s):

    return c

    base = n / (tower_const(s) * 2 ** (3**s))

def cube_gap(z: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    return 3 * z**2 + 3 * z + 1

/* ---------- exact integer arithmetic with BigInt ---------- */
function icbrt(n){                      // floor(n^(1/3)) for BigInt n >= 0

  while(hi*hi*hi <= n) hi <<= 1n;
  while(lo < hi){
    const mid = (lo + hi + 1n) >> 1n;
    if(mid*mid*mid <= n) lo = mid; else hi = mid - 1n;

}

  el('y').max = String(Number(R.y2 - R.y1) - 1);

    + `2t⁹ = ${fmt(R.z1)} ≤ z < ${fmt(R.z2)}      (t¹⁹ = ${fmt(BigInt(t)**19n)} points)`;
}

function render(){
  const t = +el('t').value, R = boxRanges(t);
  const x = BigInt(el('x').value);
  const y = R.y1 + BigInt(el('y').value);
  const z = R.z1 + BigInt(el('z').value);
  el('xval').textContent = fmt(x);
  el('yval').textContent = fmt(y);
  el('zval').textContent = fmt(z);

  const n = x**3n + y**3n + z**3n;
  el('nval').textContent = fmt(n);

  const c1 = x**3n < gap(y), c2 = x**3n + y**3n < gap(z);
  el('g1').innerHTML = `<span class="pill ${c1?'ok':'fail'}">${c1?'satisfied':'violated'}</span>`
      + `<div class="note mono">${fmt(x**3n)} vs ${fmt(gap(y))}</div>`;
  el('g2').innerHTML = `<span class="pill ${c2?'ok':'fail'}">${c2?'satisfied':'violated'}</span>`
      + `<div class="note mono">${fmt(x**3n + y**3n)} vs ${fmt(gap(z))}</div>`;

  /* greedy peel */
  const z2 = icbrt(n), r2 = n - z2**3n;
  const y2 = icbrt(r2), r1 = r2 - y2**3n;
  const x2 = icbrt(r1), rest = r1 - x2**3n;
  const rows = [
    ['leading', 'z', z2, r2, 'take the integer cube root of n and subtract its cube'],
    ['middle',  'y', y2, r1, 'take the integer cube root of the remainder and subtract'],
    ['last',    'x', x2, rest, 'what is left must itself be a perfect cube']
  ];
  el('peel').innerHTML = rows.map(([tag,name,d,rem,txt]) => `
    <div class="digit">
      <div class="tag">${tag} digit</div>
      <div><b>${name} = ${fmt(d)}</b>  ·  remainder ${fmt(rem)}
      <div class="note">${txt}</div></div>
    </div>`).join('');

  const exact = (x2 === x && y2 === y && z2 === z && rest === 0n);
  el('verdict').innerHTML = exact
    ? `<span class="pill ok">recovered exactly</span> the peel returned (x, y, z) = (${fmt(x2)}, ${fmt(y2)}, ${fmt(z2)}) — the map is invertible here, so this value is counted once and only once.`
    : `<span class="pill fail">decoding mismatch</span> the peel returned (${fmt(x2)}, ${fmt(y2)}, ${fmt(z2)}) with leftover ${fmt(rest)}, not the triple you chose. Outside the windows the gap conditions fail and the cube digits are no longer determined by the value — which is exactly why the windows are needed.`;
}

function table(){
  const rows = [];
  for(let t=2;t<=10;t++){
    const T = BigInt(t), pts = T**19n, N = 36n*(T**27n), sq = bigintSqrt(N);
    rows.push(`<tr><td>${t}</td><td>${fmt(pts)}</td><td>${fmt(N)}</td><td>${fmt(sq)}</td>
      <td>${(Number(pts)/Number(sq)).toPrecision(4)}</td></tr>`);
  }
  document.querySelector('#cmp tbody').innerHTML = rows.join('');
}
function bigintSqrt(n){
  if(n < 2n) return n;
  let lo = 0n, hi = 1n;
  while(hi*hi <= n) hi <<= 1n;
  while(lo < hi){
    const mid = (lo + hi + 1n) >> 1n;
    if(mid*mid <= n) lo = mid; else hi = mid - 1n;
  }
  return lo;
}

  render();
}));
el('rand').onclick = () => {

  el('x').value = 1 + Math.floor(Math.random()*Number(R.x2));

  el('z').value = Math.floor(Math.random()*Number(R.z2 - R.z1));
  render();
};
el('corner').onclick = () => {
  const t = +el('t').value, R = boxRanges(t);
  el('free').checked = false; refreshRanges();
  el('x').value = String(Number(R.x2));
  el('y').value = String(Number(R.y2 - R.y1) - 1);
  el('z').value = String(Number(R.z2 - R.z1) - 1);
  render();
};

refreshRanges(); render(); table();
</script>
